summary:
Jordan does not criminalise same-sex relations. The colonial-era ban was abolished by the 1951 Penal Code, which legalised private, adult, consensual same-sex acts with an age of consent of 18 regardless of gender or orientation, and no statute criminalises gender expression as such. That legal baseline does not translate into safety. Human Rights Watch reported on 6 June 2024 that authorities in Jordan, Egypt and Kuwait substitute public-morality and debauchery provisions for formal criminalisation, using them to harass LGBT people where same-sex conduct is not explicitly prohibited.

Legal gender recognition has no clear pathway. Intersex people can change official gender markers, transgender people cannot; OutRight International records the change as available only "in some cases." The Court of Cassation's ruling in Case No. 2092/2014 permitted a plaintiff born in 1977 to change name and gender from male to female in official records after hormone therapy and surgery undertaken in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically, with the court justifying the change by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex.

Gender-affirming healthcare is restricted for transgender patients and carries risk for providers. OutRight International states that such surgery is permitted for intersex people but criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018. CAIRO 52's case analysis describes the same statute as criminalising sex reassignment with penalties of up to ten years' imprisonment except in intersex cases, and separately reports that gender-affirming healthcare is penalised for providers under medical-liability law.

Online expression is exposed. Authorities promulgated a new cybercrime law in August 2023 that can target digital content on gender and sexuality as well as activists advocating LGBT rights; Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 records that the law undermines free speech and privacy online, and that peaceful dissidents and journalists were arrested and harassed under vague laws alongside intrusive digital surveillance. CAIRO 52 reports that new legislation curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access. These instruments shape what visitors as well as residents post, message and browse.

Authorities have targeted LGBT activists directly. Human Rights Watch reported on 4 December 2023 that Jordanian authorities systematically targeted LGBT rights activists in a coordinated crackdown on free expression and assembly around gender and sexuality, with officials smearing activists online by sexual orientation, social-media users posting their photographs alongside messages inciting violence, and two LGBT organisation directors citing official intimidation. Security forces also coerced queer community spaces into closing, pushing transgender and queer people to leave the country, and several organisations shut down, halted activities or saw their staff flee.
tangentialFactors:
The 2018 Medical and Health Liability Law is drafted around "changing of sex" versus "correction of sex," language broad enough that doctors performing gender-affirming surgery risk prosecution. This is a constraint on care rather than on the visitor directly, but it determines whether competent providers are available locally.

Press and publication rules form part of the same regime: the Press and Publication Law, amended in 1998 and 2004, replaced an explicit ban on depicting "sexual perversion" with a requirement that the press respect the values of the Arab and Islamic nation, giving regulators a vaguer but usable basis for restricting LGBT content. Human Rights Watch's April 2018 regional report "Audacity in Adversity" catalogues the laws used across the Middle East and North Africa to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression, and places Jordan within that wider pattern.

Social climate bears on street-level risk. A 2019 Arab Barometer survey found that 93 percent of Jordanians said society should not accept homosexuality, and vague morality laws give security forces and private individuals licence to target LGBT people with impunity, as Human Rights Watch found in its 2023 reporting. The legal abolition of same-sex criminalisation therefore coexists with low social acceptance and substantial discretionary enforcement.
localsOnly:
The government tolerates a small number of cafés in Amman that are widely considered gay-friendly. Books@Cafe, opened in 1997, remains a popular bookstore and café for patrons supportive of creativity, diversity and tolerance, though this tolerance is informal rather than codified.

LGBT publishing has a domestic history. My.Kali, described as the first LGBTQ publication in the Middle East and North Africa region, launched in 2007 and has been online since 2008, operating in the environment of digital surveillance and cybercrime legislation described above.

Despite state repression and stigma, Human Rights Watch's 2018 regional reporting found that LGBT people in the region are speaking out, building alliances and sustaining regional movements; Jordan's own activist organisations were among those forced to suspend activity or relocate staff after the December 2023 crackdown.

Honor killings were removed as a legal justification for murder under the 2013 revised Penal Code. That reform addresses violence within families and is relevant to LGBT residents whose relationships or presentation provoke family responses.
outOfScopeNotes:
Sources diverge on the precise reach of Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law (25) of 2018. OutRight International describes gender-affirming surgery as criminalised for transgender people, while CAIRO 52's case analysis states that Jordanian legislation criminalises sex reassignment with penalties of up to ten years' imprisonment except in intersex cases; a separate CAIRO 52 entry characterises the 2018 law as vaguely outlawing "changing of sex" while legalising "correction of sex." The exact statutory wording, the applicable penalty and whether the ten-year figure derives from this statute or from an older provision remain unresolved in the available inventory.

OutRight International records gender-marker change as possible "in some cases" without defining the criteria, while CAIRO 52 states flatly that transgender people cannot change markers and intersex people can. Whether any administrative route exists for transgender Jordanians, and on what conditions, is not settled by these sources.

None of the inventory sources address entry or visa screening, airport document checks, or whether gender markers on foreign passports affect admission to Jordan. No source describes official screening procedures that risk disclosing a traveller's trans status at the border.

The inventory does not state whether Jordan recognises same-sex partnerships, marriages or foreign same-sex unions, nor whether any anti-discrimination or hate-crime provisions cover gender identity or sexual orientation. These are not sourced either way.
